Scarce

/skairs/ — rhymes with bears · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Scarce describes something that is in short supply and hard to find or obtain.

Fresh vegetables were scarce in the mountain village during winter.

Worked Example

During the pandemic, face masks were scarce on store shelves, and people drove from town to town hunting for them.

Scarce emphasizes both the shortage and the difficulty in finding something. It captures that active hunt for hard-to-locate items—more precise than plain 'rare' or 'limited,' which don't capture the struggle to obtain.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

rare: Rare is about how seldom something turns up — a rare coin, a rare disease. Scarce is about supply right now: too little of something to go around, so people hunt for it. Clean water is never rare, but in a drought it becomes scarce.

limited: Limited means restricted to a small, fixed amount, often on purpose — limited seating, a limited edition of a book. Scarce says the shortage pinches: something people need is hard to find or obtain. A limit is set and known in advance; scarcity is discovered at the empty shelf.

sparse: Sparse describes how things are spread out — thin and scattered over an area, like sparse grass or sparse traffic. Scarce describes how hard something is to get: supply has run short and people struggle to obtain it. A sparse crowd is not scarce; the people simply sit far apart.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

plentiful: existing in large, generous amounts

ample: more than enough for what is needed

Where it sits · how much of it still exists — common → available → scarce → extinct

common vs. scarce: Common sits at the opposite end of the scale from scarce: common things turn up everywhere, while scarce things are in short supply and hard to find.

available vs. scarce: Available is much weaker than scarce — available simply means you can get something, while scarce warns that very little of it remains anywhere.

extinct vs. scarce: Extinct is far stronger than scarce: a scarce animal is rare but still exists, while an extinct one is gone forever, with none left at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — scars

Root — scars: plucked out; sparing, in short supply (Old North French (from Vulgar Latin *excarpsus, 'plucked out'))

Put it together

Put it together: Scarce comes from an Old North French word meaning 'plucked out' or 'sparing' — as if most of the supply had already been picked away, leaving only a little behind. That picture of a picked-over supply lives on in scarce: in short supply and hard to find or obtain.

Use the root in a new word: scarcity

Use the root in a new word: scarcity: During the drought, the scarcity of clean water forced the town to ration every drop — scarcity is simply the noun built directly on scarce.

Word Building

Word Choice

neutral / everyday

Scarce is a straightforward, accessible word for shortage or rarity—use it when something is hard to find or in limited supply. For quantity-focused contexts, 'limited' is clearer; for formal settings, 'rare' may fit better.
